sentences.chinese: 一曰，水歲多雞死及為怪，亦是也。
sentences.literal: One explanation says: In years when water dominates, many chickens die and prodigious anomalies occur—this too counts.
sentences.idiomatic: Another gloss holds that water-phase years bring mass deaths among fowl and strange portents—and that belongs here as well.

sentences.chinese: 上失威儀，則有強臣害君上者，故有下體生於上之痾。
sentences.literal: When those above lose dignity of bearing, there will be powerful ministers who harm the sovereign; hence there are ailments of the lower body appearing upon the upper.
sentences.idiomatic: When superiors forfeit proper bearing, strong ministers wound the ruler—which yields the prodigy of “lower members sprouting on the upper body.”

sentences.chinese: 木色青，故有青眚青祥。
sentences.literal: The color of wood is green; hence there are green calamities (qing sheng) and green auspices (qing xiang).
sentences.idiomatic: Wood’s hue is green, which is why green blights and green omens appear.

sentences.chinese: 凡貌傷者病木氣，木氣病則金沴之，沖氣相通也。
sentences.literal: Generally, when bearing is impaired it sickens the qi of wood; when the qi of wood is sick, metal harms it—the clashing qi communicate with one another.
sentences.idiomatic: Whenever demeanor falters, the wood phase suffers; when wood ails, metal strikes it—the two opposing forces interact.

sentences.chinese: 于《易》，《震》在東方，為春為木；
sentences.literal: In the Changes, Zhen lies in the east; it stands for spring and for wood.
sentences.idiomatic: In the Book of Changes, the trigram Zhen is placed in the east—it signifies spring and wood.

sentences.chinese: 《兌》在西方，為秋為金；
sentences.literal: Dui lies in the west; it stands for autumn and for metal.
sentences.idiomatic: Dui belongs to the west—it signifies autumn and metal.

sentences.chinese: 《離》在南方，為夏為火；
sentences.literal: Li lies in the south; it stands for summer and for fire.
sentences.idiomatic: Li belongs to the south—it signifies summer and fire.

sentences.chinese: 《坎》在北方，為冬為水。
sentences.literal: Kan lies in the north; it stands for winter and for water.
sentences.idiomatic: Kan belongs to the north—it signifies winter and water.

sentences.chinese: 春與秋日夜分，寒暑平，是以金木之氣易以相變，故貌傷則致秋陰常雨，言傷則致春陽常旱也。
sentences.literal: In spring and autumn day and night are evenly divided and cold and heat are balanced; therefore the qi of metal and wood readily transform each other; hence injury to bearing brings autumn gloom and constant rain, injury to speech brings spring sunshine and constant drought.
sentences.idiomatic: Spring and autumn balance day and night and level cold with heat, so metal and wood readily trade influence—thus impaired bearing yields endless autumn rains, while impaired speech yields spring drought beneath a glaring sun.

sentences.chinese: 至於冬夏，日夜相反，寒暑殊絕，水火之氣不得相並，故視傷常燠、聽傷常寒者，其氣然也。
sentences.literal: As for winter and summer, day and night are opposed and cold and heat are utterly different; the qi of water and fire cannot stand together; hence injury to sight brings constant warmth and injury to hearing brings constant cold—their qi are thus.
sentences.idiomatic: Winter and summer invert day and night and separate cold from heat so sharply that water and fire cannot mingle—so impaired sight trends warm and impaired hearing trends cold: that is how their phases behave.

sentences.chinese: 逆之，其極曰惡；
sentences.literal: If one opposes it, its culmination is called “evil.”
sentences.idiomatic: Defy the pattern, and the extreme is named evil.

sentences.chinese: 順之，其福曰攸好德。
sentences.literal: If one follows it, its blessing is called “that fondness for virtue.”
sentences.idiomatic: Follow it, and the blessing is “delight in virtue.”

sentences.chinese: 劉歆《貌傳》曰有鱗蟲之孽，羊禍，鼻痾。
sentences.literal: Liu Xin’s “Treatise on Bearing” says there are calamities of scale-covered creatures, sheep disasters, and ailments of the nose.
sentences.idiomatic: Liu Xin’s Treatise on Bearing lists prodigies among scaly creatures, sheep omens, and nasal deformities.

sentences.chinese: 說以為于天文東方辰為龍星，故為鱗蟲。
sentences.literal: The explanation holds that in astrology the eastern chen is the Dragon Star; hence they count as scale-covered creatures.
sentences.idiomatic: The gloss identifies the eastern asterism chen as the Dragon Star—hence “scaly creatures.”

sentences.chinese: 于《易》，《兌》為羊，木為金所病，故致羊禍，與常雨同應。
sentences.literal: In the Changes, Dui represents sheep; wood is overcome by metal; hence it brings sheep disasters, responding together with constant rain.
sentences.idiomatic: In the Changes Dui signifies sheep; wood falls ill to metal—hence sheep calamities that align with ceaseless rain.

sentences.chinese: 此說非是。
sentences.literal: This explanation is not correct.
sentences.idiomatic: That reading is wrong.

sentences.chinese: 春與秋氣陰陽相敵，木病金盛，故能相並，惟此一事耳。
sentences.literal: In spring and autumn yin and yang are evenly matched; wood is sick and metal prevails; hence they can interact—only in this one case.
sentences.idiomatic: Only in spring and autumn do yin and yang contend as equals, with enfeebled wood under dominant metal, so the phases can combine—nowhere else.

sentences.chinese: 禍與妖痾祥眚同類，不得獨異。
sentences.literal: Disasters belong with prodigies, ailments, auspices, and calamities of the same kind; they cannot be treated as uniquely different.
sentences.idiomatic: Calamities sit on the same spectrum as prodigies, lesions, omens, and blights—you cannot set them apart.

sentences.chinese: 魏尚書鄧颺揚行步馳縱，筋不束體，坐起傾倚，若無手足，此貌之不恭也。
sentences.literal: Among Wei, Minister Deng Yang’s gait was reckless and unbridled, sinews failing to bind his frame; sitting or rising he leaned and tilted as if he had no hands or feet—this was irreverence of bearing.
sentences.idiomatic: Deng Yang of Wei, a Secretariat director, walked with a loose, racing stride—his sinews seemed not to hold his body; he slumped when he sat or rose as though limbless: irreverence of demeanor.

sentences.chinese: 管輅謂之鬼躁。
sentences.literal: Guan Lu called it “ghost agitation.”
sentences.idiomatic: Guan Lu dubbed it “demon restlessness.”

sentences.chinese: 鬼躁者，凶終之徵，後卒誅也。
sentences.literal: “Ghost agitation” is a portent of a violent end; later he was executed.
sentences.idiomatic: “Ghost restlessness” foretells a bloody finish—he was put to death in the end.

sentences.chinese: 惠帝元康中，貴遊子弟相與為散發倮身之飲，對弄婢妾，逆之者傷好，非之者負譏，希世之士恥不與焉。
sentences.literal: In Emperor Hui’s Yuan-kang era, noble youths together held drinking parties with hair loosened and bodies bare, sporting with concubine-maids before one another; whoever opposed them injured friendships, whoever criticized them bore ridicule, and men seeking fame were ashamed not to join.
sentences.idiomatic: Under Emperor Hui in the Yuan-kang years, young aristocrats threw banquets with hair unbound and skins naked, fondling servant girls in plain sight; crossing them cost goodwill, criticizing them earned jeers, and career-minded men were ashamed to stay away.

sentences.chinese: 蓋貌之不恭，胡狄侵中國之萌也。
sentences.literal: This was irreverence of bearing—the first sprouting of northern tribes invading the Central Plains.
sentences.idiomatic: It was bearing without dignity—the first stirrings of steppe peoples overrunning China.

sentences.chinese: 其後遂有五胡之亂，此又失在狂也。
sentences.literal: Afterward there came the turmoil of the Five Hu—this again lay in the fault called frenzy.
sentences.idiomatic: The Five Hu upheaval followed—another case of the “madness” failing.

sentences.chinese: 元康中，賈謐親貴，數入二宮，與儲君遊戲，無降下心。
sentences.literal: In Yuan-kang, Jia Mi was honored as kin, entered the two inner palaces repeatedly, and played games with the heir apparent, showing no mind of submission.
sentences.idiomatic: During Yuan-kang, Jia Mi enjoyed imperial favor: he kept slipping into the two palaces to amuse the crown prince and never lowered himself in deference.

sentences.chinese: 又嘗因弈棋爭道，成都王穎厲色曰：「皇太子國之儲貳，賈謐何敢無禮！
sentences.literal: Moreover he once quarreled over a weiqi move; the Prince of Chengdu, Sima Ying, said sternly: “The imperial heir is the nation’s successor—how dare Jia Mi be rude!
sentences.idiomatic: Once, disputing a chess placement, Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, snapped: “The crown prince is the realm’s reserve—how dare Jia Mi lack respect!

sentences.chinese: 」謐猶不悛，故及於禍，貌不恭之罰也。
sentences.literal: ” Jia Mi still did not reform, hence he met disaster—the punishment for irreverence of bearing.
sentences.idiomatic: ” Yet Jia Mi refused to mend his ways and paid with his life—the reckoning for disrespectful bearing.

sentences.chinese: 齊王冏既誅趙王倫，因留輔政，坐拜百官，符敕臺府，淫醟專驕，不一朝覲，此狂恣不肅之咎也。
sentences.literal: Prince Qi, Sima Jiong, having executed Prince Zhao, Sima Lun, remained to assist governance: seated he invested the hundred officials, issued edicts from terrace offices, drowned in wine and sole arrogance, and never once attended court—this was the fault of mad presumption and want of solemnity.
sentences.idiomatic: After killing Prince Zhao Sima Lun, Prince Qi Sima Jiong stayed as regent: he handed out posts from his seat, ran the ministries by decree, reveled in wine and pride, and skipped every audience—mad impudence with no dignity.

sentences.chinese: 天下莫不高其功而慮其亡也，冏終弗改，遂致夷滅。
sentences.literal: None under Heaven failed to honor his merit yet dread his ruin; Jiong to the end did not reform, and so met extinction.
sentences.idiomatic: The realm praised his deed yet feared his fall; Jiong never changed—and was wiped out.

sentences.chinese: 司馬道子於府園內列肆，使姬人酤鬻，身自貿易。
sentences.literal: Sima Daozi set out market stalls in his manor garden, had concubines sell ale, and traded in person.
sentences.idiomatic: Sima Daozi lined his estate with shops, put concubines behind the counter, and haggled himself.

sentences.chinese: 干寶以為貴者失位，降在皁隸之象也。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao took it as the image of the noble losing position and descending among dark-clad servants.
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao read it as rank pulled down among common hirelings.

sentences.chinese: 俄而道子見廢，以庶人終，此貌不恭之應也。
sentences.literal: Soon Daozi was deposed and ended as a commoner—this responded to irreverence of bearing.
sentences.idiomatic: Daozi was soon stripped of office and died a commoner—the sign answering irreverent bearing.

sentences.chinese: 安帝，將拜授劉毅世子，毅以王命之重，當設饗宴，親請吏佐臨視。
sentences.literal: Emperor An, about to invest Liu Yi’s son as heir, Liu Yi—because the royal command was weighty—ought to have laid a feast and personally invited clerks to oversee it.
sentences.idiomatic: When Emperor An was to ennoble Liu Yi’s heir, Liu Yi—because the imperial commission mattered—should have spread a banquet and brought his staff to witness it.

sentences.chinese: 至拜日，國僚不重白，默拜於廄中。
sentences.literal: On the day of investiture, his household colleagues did not report upward again; they silently performed the rite in the stable.
sentences.idiomatic: Come the ceremony, his officers never cleared it upstairs; they muttered the investiture inside the stables.

sentences.chinese: 王人將反命，毅方知之，大以為恨，免郎中令劉敬叔官。
sentences.literal: When the king’s envoy was about to return his report, Liu Yi only then learned of it, greatly resented it, and dismissed Director of Gentlemen of the Palace Liu Jingshu.
sentences.idiomatic: The imperial messenger was nearly on the road back before Liu Yi heard—he was furious and cashiered Liu Jingshu, director of the gentlemen-of-the-palace.

sentences.chinese: 天戒若曰，此惰略嘉禮不肅之妖也。
sentences.literal: Heaven’s warning seemed to say: this was the prodigy of lazily slighting a splendid rite and lacking solemnity.
sentences.idiomatic: Heaven warned: skimping on a sacred ceremony without gravity yields this portent.

sentences.chinese: 其後毅遂被殺焉。
sentences.literal: Afterward Liu Yi was then killed.
sentences.idiomatic: Liu Yi was executed soon after.

sentences.chinese: 庶征恆雨，劉歆以為《春秋》大雨，劉向以為大水。
sentences.literal: Among the miscellaneous signs, constant rain—Liu Xin took it as “great rain” in the Spring and Autumn; Liu Xiang as “great flood.”
sentences.idiomatic: Under “miscellaneous omens,” endless rain: Liu Xin reads the Spring and Autumn’s “great rains”; Liu Xiang reads catastrophic flood.

sentences.chinese: 魏明帝秋，數大雨，多暴卒，雷電非常，至殺鳥雀。
sentences.literal: In Wei Mingdi’s autumn it rained heavily many times; many died suddenly; thunder and lightning were extraordinary, even killing birds.
sentences.idiomatic: One autumn under Wei’s Mingdi the skies opened repeatedly; people dropped dead; lightning flashed unnaturally, killing even small birds.

sentences.chinese: 案楊阜上疏，此恆雨之罰也。
sentences.literal: According to Yang Fu’s memorial, this was the punishment of constant rain.
sentences.idiomatic: Yang Fu’s memorial treats it as the scourge of ceaseless rain.

sentences.chinese: 時天子居喪不哀，出入弋獵無度，奢侈繁興，奪農時，故水失其性而恆雨為罰。
sentences.literal: At the time the Son of Heaven in mourning was not mournful, went out and in hunting without limit, luxury flourished in profusion, and farming seasons were seized; hence water lost its nature and constant rain served as punishment.
sentences.idiomatic: The emperor wore mourning without grief, hunted without restraint, lavished wealth, and stole time from the fields—water lost its proper character, and unending rain was the penalty.

sentences.chinese: 八月，大雨霖三十餘日，伊、洛、河、漢皆溢，歲以凶饑。
sentences.literal: In the eighth month, great rain fell more than thirty days; the Yi, Luo, Yellow River, and Han all overflowed; the year saw famine.
sentences.idiomatic: For over thirty days in the eighth month torrents fell; the Yi, Luo, Yellow River, and Han burst their banks; the harvest failed and hunger spread.

sentences.chinese: 吳孫亮二月甲寅，大雨，震電。
sentences.literal: Wu’s Sun Liang, second month, day jiayin: great rain, thunder and lightning.
sentences.idiomatic: On jiayin of the second month under Wu’s Sun Liang came deluges and lightning.

sentences.chinese: 乙卯，雪，大寒。
sentences.literal: Yimao: snow, great cold.
sentences.idiomatic: The next day, yimao: snow and bitter cold.

sentences.chinese: 案劉歆說，此時當雨而不當大，大雨，恆雨之罰也。
sentences.literal: According to Liu Xin’s doctrine, at this season it ought to rain but not heavily; heavy rain is the punishment of constant rain.
sentences.idiomatic: Liu Xin argues it should have sprinkled then—a deluge instead marks the “constant rain” scourge.

sentences.chinese: 於始震電之，明日而雪，大寒，又常寒之罰也。
sentences.literal: At first thunder and lightning; the next day snow, great cold—again the punishment of constant cold.
sentences.idiomatic: Lightning first, then snow and killing frost the day after—another stroke of “constant cold.”

sentences.chinese: 劉向以為既已雷電，則雪不當復降，皆失時之異也。
sentences.literal: Liu Xiang held that once there had been thunder and lightning, snow ought not to fall again—all were anomalies of mistimed seasons.
sentences.idiomatic: Liu Xiang thought lightning should rule out more snow—each event arrived out of season.

sentences.chinese: 天戒若曰，為君失時，賊臣將起。
sentences.literal: Heaven’s warning seemed to say: the ruler loses the seasons; traitorous ministers will arise.
sentences.idiomatic: Heaven warned: mistiming sovereignty breeds rebellious ministers.

sentences.chinese: 先震電而後雪者，陰見間隙，起而勝陽，逆弑之禍將成也。
sentences.literal: Thunder and lightning first and snow afterward means yin saw an opening, rose, and overcame yang—the disaster of usurpation and regicide will take shape.
sentences.idiomatic: Lightning then snow means yin spied a gap, surged, and mastered yang—the blade and coup draw near.

sentences.chinese: 亮不悟，尋見廢。
sentences.literal: Liang did not understand; soon he was deposed.
sentences.idiomatic: Sun Liang never saw it—soon he was cast down.

sentences.chinese: 此與《春秋》魯隱同。
sentences.literal: This matches Duke Yin of Lu in the Spring and Autumn.
sentences.idiomatic: It parallels the Spring and Autumn record for Duke Yin of Lu.

sentences.chinese: 武帝六月，大雨霖。
sentences.literal: Emperor Wu, sixth month: great soaking rain.
sentences.idiomatic: In Emperor Wu’s sixth month the rains would not stop.

sentences.chinese: 甲辰，河、洛、伊、沁水同時並溢，流四千九百餘家，殺二百餘人，沒秋稼千三百六十餘頃。
sentences.literal: Jiachen: the Yellow River, Luo, Yi, and Qin streams overflowed together, swept four thousand nine hundred-odd households, killed two hundred-odd people, and submerged autumn crops over thirteen hundred sixty qing.
sentences.idiomatic: On jiachen the Yellow River, Luo, Yi, and Qin floods crested as one, washing away nearly five thousand homes, killing over two hundred, and drowning more than 1,360 qing of autumn grain.

sentences.chinese: 七月，任城、梁國暴雨，害豆麥。
sentences.literal: Seventh month: Ren-cheng and Liang-nation violent rain, harming beans and wheat.
sentences.idiomatic: In the seventh month Ren-cheng and Liang were hit by cloudbursts that ruined beans and wheat.

sentences.chinese: 九月，南安郡霖雨暴雪，樹木摧折，害秋稼。
sentences.literal: Ninth month: Nan-an commandery unending rain and violent snow; trees snapped; autumn crops were harmed.
sentences.idiomatic: Nan-an commandery endured weeks of rain and blizzard that shattered trees and spoiled the autumn harvest.

sentences.chinese: 是秋，魏郡西平郡九縣、淮南、平原霖雨暴水，霜傷秋稼。
sentences.literal: That autumn, nine counties of Wei commandery and Xi-ping commandery, Huai-nan, and Ping-yuan saw soaking rain and sudden floods; frost injured autumn crops.
sentences.idiomatic: That fall, nine counties across Wei and Xi-ping along with Huai-nan and Ping-yuan were flooded; late frost ruined the crops.

sentences.chinese: 惠帝十月、義陽、南陽、東海霖雨，淹害秋麥。
sentences.literal: Emperor Hui, tenth month: Yi-yang, Nan-yang, and Dong-hai soaking rain, inundating and harming autumn wheat.
sentences.idiomatic: In Emperor Hui’s tenth month relentless rain swamped Yi-yang, Nan-yang, and Dong-hai and drowned the winter wheat.

sentences.chinese: 元帝，春雨至於夏。
sentences.literal: Emperor Yuan: spring rain lasting into summer.
sentences.idiomatic: Under Emperor Yuan spring rains dragged into summer.

sentences.chinese: 是時王敦執權，不恭之罰也。
sentences.literal: At this time Wang Dun held power—the punishment of irreverence.
sentences.idiomatic: Wang Dun held the reins then—the penalty for irreverent bearing.

sentences.chinese: ，春雨四十餘日，晝夜雷電震五十餘日。
sentences.literal: , Spring rain lasted more than forty days; day and night thunder and lightning shook for more than fifty days.
sentences.idiomatic: For over forty days spring rains fell; thunder rolled night and day for more than fifty.

sentences.chinese: 是時王敦興兵，王師敗績之應也。
sentences.literal: At this time Wang Dun raised troops—this responded to the defeat of the royal army.
sentences.idiomatic: Wang Dun was marching then—the omen of the imperial army’s rout.

sentences.chinese: 成帝，春雨五十餘日，恆雷電。
sentences.literal: Emperor Cheng: spring rain more than fifty days, constant thunder and lightning.
sentences.idiomatic: Emperor Cheng’s reign brought fifty-odd days of spring rain and ceaseless thunder.

sentences.chinese: 是時雖斬蘇峻，其餘黨猶據守石頭，至其滅後，淫雨乃霽。
sentences.literal: At this time although Su Jun had been beheaded, his remaining partisans still held Stone Citadel; only after they were extinguished did the excessive rain clear.
sentences.idiomatic: Su Jun was dead but his followers still held Stone City; only when they were wiped out did the endless rain break.

sentences.chinese: 八月乙丑，荊州之長沙攸、醴陵、武陵之龍陽，三縣雨水，浮漂屋室，殺人，損秋稼。
sentences.literal: Eighth month, yichou: You county (Chang-sha), Li-ling, and Long-yang (Wu-ling)—three counties’ rainwater floated houses, killed people, and harmed autumn crops.
sentences.idiomatic: On yichou in the eighth month, downpours in You (Chang-sha), Li-ling, and Long-yang (Wu-ling) swept away homes, took lives, and ruined the autumn harvest.

sentences.chinese: 是時帝幼，權在於下。
sentences.literal: At this time the emperor was young; power lay below.
sentences.idiomatic: The sovereign was a child; real power sat beneath the throne.

sentences.literal: Equals sign used as a typographical section divider.
sentences.idiomatic: Typographical section divider.

sentences.chinese: 服妖
sentences.literal: Clothing prodigies.
sentences.idiomatic: Garment omens.

sentences.chinese: =魏武帝以天下凶荒，資財乏匱，始擬古皮弁，裁縑帛為白帢，以易舊服。
sentences.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei, because all under Heaven suffered famine and goods were scarce, first imitated the ancient leather cap, cutting silk tabby to make a white qia in place of the former dress.
sentences.idiomatic: Emperor Wu of Wei, with the realm starving and supplies exhausted, copied the old leather bonnet and tailored plain silk into a white qia to replace court headgear.

sentences.chinese: 傅玄曰；
sentences.literal: Fu Xuan said;
sentences.idiomatic: Fu Xuan observed:

sentences.chinese: 「白乃軍容，非國容也。
sentences.literal: “White is military dress, not court dress.
sentences.idiomatic: “White belongs on campaign, not in state ritual.

sentences.chinese: 」干寶以為「縞素，凶喪之象也」。
sentences.literal: ” Gan Bao held that “plain white silk is the image of death and mourning.”
sentences.idiomatic: ” Gan Bao read it as “bleached cloth signals bereavement.”

sentences.chinese: 名之為帢，毀辱之言也，蓋革代之後，劫殺之妖也。
sentences.literal: Naming it qia is language of insult and ruin; after the change of mandate it was the prodigy of robbery and slaughter.
sentences.idiomatic: Calling it a qia was mockery—a portent of usurpation and bloodshed after the throne changed hands.

sentences.chinese: 魏明帝著繡帽，披縹紈半袖，常以見直臣楊阜，諫曰：「此禮何法服邪！
sentences.literal: Wei Mingdi wore an embroidered cap and draped a half-sleeve of sky-blue tabby; he often wore it to audience the upright minister Yang Fu, who remonstrated: “What ritual norm of dress is this!
sentences.idiomatic: Mingdi of Wei sported an embroidered hat and a sky-blue half-sleeve; he wore them to see the upright Yang Fu, who protested: “What canonical garment is this!

sentences.chinese: 」帝默然。
sentences.literal: ” The emperor was silent.
sentences.idiomatic: ” The emperor had no reply.

sentences.chinese: 近服妖也。
sentences.literal: This bordered on clothing prodigy.
sentences.idiomatic: It skirted a garment omen.

sentences.chinese: 夫縹，非禮之色。
sentences.literal: Now sky-blue is not a color sanctioned by ritual.
sentences.idiomatic: Sky-blue is not a ritual hue.

sentences.chinese: 褻服尚不以紅紫，況接臣下乎？
sentences.literal: Even intimate garments do not use red and purple—how much more when receiving ministers below?
sentences.idiomatic: Undress eschews forbidden reds and purples—how dare court robes flout them before ministers?

sentences.chinese: 人主親禦非法之章，所謂自作孽不可禳也。
sentences.literal: The ruler personally assumes unlawful insignia—what is called self-made calamity cannot be expiated.
sentences.idiomatic: When the sovereign dons unlawful regalia, he courts a doom no rite can lift.

sentences.chinese: 帝既不享永年，身沒而祿去王室，後嗣不終，遂亡天下。
sentences.literal: The emperor did not enjoy long years; his person gone and stipends departed from the royal house, posterity did not reach its term, and so all under Heaven was lost.
sentences.idiomatic: He gained no long reign; dead, his line lost the mandate—his heirs did not endure, and the realm slipped away.

sentences.chinese: ，發銅鑄為巨人二，號曰翁仲，置之司馬門外。
sentences.literal: , They melted copper to cast two giants, called them Wengzhong, and placed them outside the Sima Gate.
sentences.idiomatic: Bronze was recast into two colossal statues dubbed Wengzhong and set outside the Sima Gate.

sentences.chinese: 案古長人見，為國亡。
sentences.literal: According to antiquity, when tall men appear, it is for the state’s perishing.
sentences.idiomatic: Ancient precedent says giants foretell a kingdom’s end.

sentences.chinese: 長狄見臨洮，為秦亡之禍。
sentences.literal: The Long Di appeared at Lintao—disaster for Qin’s perishing.
sentences.idiomatic: The Long Di at Lintao spelled Qin’s doom.

sentences.chinese: 始皇不悟，反以為嘉祥，鑄銅人以象之。
sentences.literal: The First Emperor did not understand; instead he took it as auspicious omen and cast bronze men to image them.
sentences.idiomatic: The First Emperor misread the sign as blessing and cast bronze giants in their likeness.

sentences.chinese: 魏法亡國之器，而於義竟無取焉。
sentences.literal: Wei copied the device of a perishing state, and in rectitude it ultimately took nothing.
sentences.idiomatic: Wei copied a dying dynasty’s stunt—to no moral purpose.

sentences.chinese: 蓋服妖也。
sentences.literal: This was clothing prodigy.
sentences.idiomatic: Another garment omen.

sentences.chinese: 尚書何晏好服婦人之服，傅玄曰：「此妖服也。
sentences.literal: Minister He Yan liked to wear women’s dress; Fu Xuan said: “This is prodigy dress.
sentences.idiomatic: Director He Yan favored women’s clothing; Fu Xuan said: “This is omen dress.

sentences.chinese: 夫衣裳之制，所以定上下殊內外也。
sentences.literal: The system of upper and lower garments is how one fixes superiors and inferiors and distinguishes inner from outer.
sentences.idiomatic: Robes exist to set high against low and inside against outside.

sentences.chinese: 《大雅》云『玄袞赤舄，鉤膺鏤錫』，歌其文也。
sentences.literal: The Greater Odes says, “Dark robe and red shoes, hooked breastplate and carved bells”—it sings its pattern.
sentences.idiomatic: The Greater Odes exclaims “black robe, red slippers, hooked breast-straps, chased bells”—praising its ornament.

sentences.chinese: 《小雅》云『有嚴有翼，共武之服』，詠其武也。
sentences.literal: The Lesser Odes says, “Awesome and aiding, together in martial dress”—it chants its martial quality.
sentences.idiomatic: The Lesser Odes cries “solemn, supportive—those martial robes together”—honoring their strength.

sentences.chinese: 若內外不殊，王制失敘，服妖既作，身隨之亡。
sentences.literal: If inner and outer are not distinguished, royal regulation loses order; once clothing prodigy arises, the person follows it in death.
sentences.idiomatic: Blur inner with outer and royal order collapses; garment omens appear—and the wearer perishes.

sentences.chinese: 妹嬉冠男子之冠，桀亡天下；
sentences.literal: Mo Xi capped herself with a man’s cap—Jie lost all under Heaven;
sentences.idiomatic: Mo Xi wore a man’s crown—Jie lost the realm;

sentences.chinese: 何晏服婦人之服，亦亡其家，其咎均也。」
sentences.literal: He Yan wore women’s dress—also lost his family; the fault is equal.”
sentences.idiomatic: He Yan dressed as a woman—and lost his house; the guilt matches.”

sentences.chinese: 吳婦人修容者，急束其發而劘角過於耳，蓋其俗自操束太急，而廉隅失中之謂也。
sentences.literal: Among Wu women who adorned their faces, they tightly bound their hair and shaved the temples past the ears—this speaks of their custom binding itself too tight and of corners losing the mean.
sentences.idiomatic: Wu women who styled their looks wrenched their hair tight and cropped temples past the ears—vanity pulled so taut that proportion broke.

sentences.chinese: 故吳之風俗，相驅以急，言論彈射，以刻薄相尚。
sentences.literal: Hence Wu’s customs drove one another with haste; speech shot accusations; harshness was esteemed.
sentences.idiomatic: Hence Wu’s manners chased urgency: words flew like bolts, and cruelty passed for cleverness.

sentences.chinese: 居三年之喪者，往往有致毀以死。
sentences.literal: Those observing three-year mourning often brought destruction unto death.
sentences.idiomatic: Mourners for parents often wasted away unto death.

sentences.chinese: 諸葛患之，著《正交論》，雖不可以經訓整亂，蓋亦救時之作也。
sentences.literal: Zhuge Ke worried over it and composed “Treatise on Correct Associations”; though it cannot with canonical teaching rectify chaos, it is also a work to rescue the times.
sentences.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke fretted and wrote On Proper Associations—not scripture enough to cure chaos, but a tract for its age.

sentences.chinese: 孫休後，衣服之制上長下短，又積領五六而裳居一二。
sentences.literal: After Sun Xiu, the cut of garments was long above and short below; moreover collars stacked five or six layers while skirts counted only one or two.
sentences.idiomatic: After Sun Xiu, fashion ran long on top and short below—five or six layered collars against one or two skirt panels.

sentences.chinese: 干寶曰：「上饒奢，下儉逼，上有餘下不足之妖也。
sentences.literal: Gan Bao said: “Above indulges luxury while below is squeezed by austerity—the prodigy of surplus above and shortage below.
sentences.idiomatic: Gan Bao said: “Extravagance reigns aloft while austerity pinches below—a portent of plenty upstairs and want downstairs.

sentences.chinese: 」至孫皓，果奢暴恣情於上，而百姓雕困于下，卒以亡國，是其應也。
sentences.literal: ” Down to Sun Hao, extravagance and cruelty indeed ran riot above while the hundred surnames were hollowed out below; the state finally perished—this was its response.
sentences.idiomatic: ” Under Sun Hao, indulgence and brutality flourished above while commoners were bled dry below; the realm fell—that was the fulfillment.

sentences.chinese: 武帝泰始初，衣服上儉下豐，著衣者皆厭䙅，此君衰弱，臣放縱，下掩上之象也。
sentences.literal: Early in Emperor Wu’s Taishi reign, garments were austere above and ample below; wearers all trailed hems—this is the image of the lord weak, ministers unrestrained, and the base overshadowing the top.
sentences.idiomatic: Early in Emperor Wu’s Taishi era, coats grew tight above and billowing below—every sleeve pooled on the floor: the sovereign enfeebled, his ministers unchecked, the base veiling the crown.
